lessons.title: Your brain runs on 20 watts
lessons.sourceVideoTitle: Your Brain Runs on 20 Watts: Here's Why Try Harder Fails
keyIdea: Your brain is about 2% of your body weight but uses about 20% of its energy, and most of that energy is spent even when you are resting.
Focusing pulls extra energy into one task. Push too long and the brain dims, and mistakes start to creep in.
Working harder is not the same as learning more. Focus in blocks, then recharge with real rest.
lessons.action: Do one focused block of 30 to 60 minutes on a single task today. Then take 10 minutes of real rest: a walk, fresh air or sunlight, not your phone.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: At what point today did your work start to slip?

quiz.question: Roughly how much of the body's energy does the brain use?
quiz.explanation: The brain is only about 2% of body weight, yet it uses around 20% of the body's energy.

quiz.question: According to the video, how long should you focus on one task before a break?
options: No more than about 60 to 90 minutes
quiz.explanation: Adeel explains our natural rhythms: focus for up to 60 to 90 minutes, less for young children, then recharge.

quiz.question: Which of these does NOT recharge your brain?
quiz.explanation: Rest, nature, sunlight, a bath or exercise help the brain recover. Screens keep it busy.

lessons.title: One thing at a time
lessons.sourceVideoTitle: Your Brain Runs on 20 Watts: Here's Why Try Harder Fails
keyIdea: Each task you focus on asks your brain for a little more energy.
A book, a phone and a TV at the same time split that energy three ways, and the load grows.
An overloaded brain misses big things: in the famous gorilla experiment, about half the viewers never saw the gorilla.
lessons.action: Pick one important task today. Put your phone in another room, switch off the TV and music, and give that task 25 minutes of single focus.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: What pulled your attention away today, and what did you do about it?

quiz.question: What happens when you split your focus across several things at once?
options: The load on the brain grows and you miss more
quiz.explanation: Every extra focus point adds load. An overloaded brain starts missing obvious things.

quiz.question: In the gorilla experiment, what were viewers asked to do?
options: Count the passes of the ball
quiz.explanation: They were busy counting basketball passes, and about half never noticed a gorilla walking through.

quiz.question: Which set-up best helps focus?
options: One task, phone away, no background screens
quiz.explanation: Adeel's advice: when you focus, focus on one thing, with no phone, music or TV alongside.

lessons.title: Try it yourself first
lessons.sourceVideoTitle: A Science Based New Way to Study | Neuroplasticity | Episode 19
keyIdea: Start by skimming: look quickly over the chapter or skill so you know what is where.
Then try a question on your own, with no hints, no Google and no help. The struggle is what builds your brain's 'muscles'.
Only after you have tried, check your answer and correct your mistakes.
lessons.action: Choose one problem, task or skill today. Attempt it completely on your own before you look anything up. Then check and fix your answer.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: What did you try on your own today, and what did checking your answer teach you?

quiz.question: What is the first step of the learning circle?
quiz.explanation: First you skim, just enough to know what is in the chapter and where.

quiz.question: Why avoid hints when you first attempt a question?
options: The struggle builds your own thinking
quiz.explanation: Taking a hint borrows the method. Working it out yourself is what makes the skill your own.

quiz.question: When should you check your answer?
options: After you have attempted it yourself
quiz.explanation: Attempt first, then check and correct. That order shows you exactly where your mistake was.

lessons.title: Rest is part of learning
lessons.sourceVideoTitle: A Science Based New Way to Study | Neuroplasticity | Episode 19
keyIdea: After each attempt, stop for 10 to 20 seconds, close your eyes and pay attention only to your breathing.
During that short, deep rest your brain quietly replays what you just practised.
Learning has two stages, focus and rest. Repeat the circle: focus, check, rest, then the next question.
lessons.action: Today, after each task, question or page, close your eyes for 20 seconds and follow your breath before moving on.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: How did the short rests change the way you felt while learning?

quiz.question: What do you do in the short rest step?
options: Close your eyes and focus on your breathing
Start the next question straight away
quiz.explanation: For 10 to 20 seconds you close your eyes, think of nothing, and follow your breath.

quiz.question: What does the brain do during that rest?
quiz.explanation: In rest the brain keeps revising what you learned, on its own.

quiz.question: What are the two stages of learning described in the video?
quiz.explanation: Adeel's summary: learning is focus, then relax, then focus again.

lessons.title: You can change your brain
keyIdea: For a long time people were told the brain cannot change, so there was little point trying to do much better.
That was a myth. At any age, your brain can change both its structure and the way it works.
If the brain can change, so can your habits. The next lessons show you practical ways to do it.
lessons.action: Write down one habit you would like to change and one new habit you would like to build. Keep the note where you will see it during the next lessons.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: Which habit did you pick, and why does it matter to you?

quiz.question: What were people told about the brain for a long time?
options: That it changes all the time
That it only changes in old age
quiz.explanation: The old belief was that the brain is fixed. Adeel calls that a myth.

quiz.question: According to the video, at what age can the brain change?
quiz.explanation: Today we know a person can change their brain at any age.

quiz.question: What can change in the brain?
options: Its structure and how it works
quiz.explanation: Both the brain's structure and its function can change. That is neuroplasticity.

lessons.title: Use it or lose it
lessons.sourceVideoTitle: Third Rule Of Neuro Plasticity | Use or Loose it
keyIdea: The third rule of neuroplasticity: the parts of the brain you use grow stronger, and the parts you stop using fade.
People who learn a second language develop denser grey matter in the language areas. If they forget the language, the brain slowly goes back.
Juggling, dancing and other rhythmic movement build the brain too, but only while you keep doing them.
lessons.action: Spend 15 minutes on something new for your brain today: a few words of a new language, three balls to juggle, or a new dance step.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: What new thing did you try today, and how did it feel?

quiz.question: What does "use it or lose it" mean for the brain?
options: Parts you use get stronger; parts you don't use fade
The brain loses cells when you use it
You should rest the brain as much as possible
quiz.explanation: Brain areas that work keep growing. Areas left unused weaken or take on other jobs.

quiz.question: What happened to grey matter when people learned another language?
quiz.explanation: Grey matter in the language areas became denser, and its shape changed.

quiz.question: What happens if you stop juggling after learning it?
quiz.explanation: Stop practising and the extra grey matter goes back to where it was.

lessons.title: A memory is a connection
keyIdea: Nobel Prize winner Eric Kandel showed that a memory is not kept in a box. It is a connection between neurons.
Repetition makes these connections stronger, so you remember things for longer.
When you seem to forget something, the connection has only gone quiet. Go through the same experience again and it often comes back.
lessons.action: Pick one thing you learned in this course. Say it out loud to someone this morning, and again in the evening, without looking at your notes.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: How much did you remember the second time compared with the first?

quiz.question: According to Eric Kandel's research, what is a memory?
options: A file stored in one box
quiz.explanation: His experiments showed that memory lives in the connections (synapses) between neurons.

quiz.question: What makes a memory connection stronger?
quiz.explanation: Each time you go over something, the connection grows stronger and lasts longer.

quiz.question: When you "forget" something, what has often happened?
options: The memory is gone for good
The connection has gone quiet for a while
quiz.explanation: The memory is inactive, not erased. Meeting the same experience again can bring it back.

lessons.title: Step out of your comfort zone
lessons.sourceVideoTitle: Out of Comfort Zone | Power of Neuroplasticity | Episode 6
keyIdea: The more your brain struggles with something unfamiliar, the more it learns.
Small, slightly uncomfortable exercises prepare the brain for change, the way ploughing prepares a field before you sow seeds.
Keep them random. Once something becomes routine, it stops stretching the brain.
lessons.action: Do one small thing differently today: take a new route, brush your teeth with your other hand, or order something you have never tried.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: What felt uncomfortable today, and what did you notice while doing it?

quiz.question: When does the brain learn the most?
options: When everything is easy and familiar
When it works through some discomfort
quiz.explanation: Adeel explains that the more the brain struggles, the more it learns.

quiz.question: What does Adeel compare these first exercises to?
quiz.explanation: Like ploughing, they prepare the ground so change can take root.

quiz.question: Why should you avoid turning these exercises into a fixed routine?
options: A routine stops challenging the brain
quiz.explanation: Do them at random. Once they are routine, they lose their purpose.

lessons.title: Make a new habit stick
lessons.sourceVideoTitle: Making New Habits Permanent | Neuroplasticity | Episode 12
keyIdea: An old habit is a short, well-worn path in the brain. A new habit starts as a long bypass, and the brain prefers the shortest road.
Each repetition makes the bypass shorter. When it is shorter than the old path, the new habit takes over and the old one fades.
Repetition is easier when the habit is linked to something you enjoy for its own sake, not only to a reward from outside.
lessons.action: Take the new habit you wrote down in Lesson 5. Link it to something you enjoy, such as walking with a friend or listening to music, and do it once today.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: What did you link your new habit to, and did it make it easier?

quiz.question: Why does the brain prefer an old habit?
options: Its path is shorter and uses less energy
The brain cannot learn new paths
quiz.explanation: The brain saves energy, so it takes the shortest, most used path.

quiz.question: What makes the new path (the bypass) shorter?
quiz.explanation: Each repetition shortens the bypass until it beats the old path.

quiz.question: Which motivation keeps a habit going longest?
options: Something you enjoy for its own sake
quiz.explanation: Rewards from outside stop when the reward stops. Joy in the process keeps you going.

lessons.title: Self-control in baby steps
keyIdea: Willpower is not fixed. Like any skill, self-control can be trained and grows with practice.
Don't start at the hardest level. Begin with a small step you can win, then raise the difficulty slowly.
To resist ice cream, first look at the shop from far away and walk home. Later go closer, then inside with a friend, and only then alone.
lessons.action: Pick one temptation you want to beat. Write three baby steps, from easy to hard, and do the first step today.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: What was your first baby step, and how did it go?

quiz.question: What does neuroscience say about willpower?
options: You are born with a fixed amount
It can be trained and increased
It only works in the morning
quiz.explanation: Self-control can be learned and grows with practice.

quiz.question: Where should you start when training self-control?
options: With a small step you can win
quiz.explanation: Start with baby steps and raise the difficulty slowly.

quiz.question: Why is ice cream such a strong temptation?
options: It triggers several senses at once
quiz.explanation: Sight, smell and taste all trigger the craving, and eating it gives a dopamine reward.

lessons.title: Write it down
lessons.sourceVideoTitle: Exercises Which can Change Brain Structure | Neuroplasticity | Episode 10
keyIdea: When you are stressed, the amygdala, a small alarm in the brain, starts ringing.
Writing your feelings down helps the alarm quieten. Studies link keeping a diary with lower stress.
Don't be shy on paper: "I am scared", "this is hard". Naming the feeling is the point.
lessons.action: Before bed, write five lines about your day: one thing that worried you, how it made you feel, and one thing that went well.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: How did you feel after writing your five lines?

quiz.question: Which part of the brain acts like an alarm under stress?
quiz.explanation: Adeel calls the amygdala the brain's bell: it starts ringing when you are stressed.

quiz.question: What does writing your feelings down do?
quiz.explanation: Putting negative feelings on paper helps the amygdala calm down.

quiz.question: What should you write in your diary?
options: Your honest feelings, even the hard ones
quiz.explanation: Name your feelings honestly. That is what helps.

lessons.title: Your brain is social
lessons.sourceVideoTitle: Ten Social Exercises for Brain | Power of Neuroplasticity | Episode 8
keyIdea: Humans have always lived, worked and learned in groups. Our brains grow through real contact with people.
Today's social age is mostly digital. We greet neighbours in passing but rarely sit and talk with them.
Simple social exercises, like meeting someone new, talking with elders or helping someone, keep that part of the brain active.
lessons.action: Have one real conversation today with someone you usually only greet: a neighbour, an older relative or a colleague. Put the phone away and listen.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: Whom did you talk to, and what did you learn from them?

quiz.question: How have humans lived through most of history?
quiz.explanation: We have always hunted, protected each other and learned in groups.

quiz.question: What is different about today's social age?
options: We meet people more than ever
It is mostly through screens, and we drift apart
It has no effect on us
quiz.explanation: Our digital footprint grows while real time with family and neighbours shrinks.

quiz.question: Which is one of Adeel's social exercises?
options: Sit with new people at a wedding
Always sit with people you know
quiz.explanation: He suggests sitting with new people at a function and meeting at least ten of them.

lessons.title: Reframe the memory
keyIdea: You can reframe a painful memory to take the sting out of it.
Put yourself in the other person's shoes. Where you see a 6, they may be looking at a 9.
Adeel was slapped at university. Only years later, seeing it through the other student's eyes, did he see his own mistake. Owning mistakes lets you learn from them.
lessons.action: Pick one memory that still bothers you. Write how the other person might have seen it, and one thing you could have done differently.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: Did seeing it from the other side change how you feel about it?

quiz.question: What is reframing?
options: Looking at a memory in a new way to take out the hurt
quiz.explanation: Reframing changes how you see a memory so the pain loses its grip.

quiz.question: What does the 6 and 9 example teach?
options: The other person may see the same thing differently
One of you must be lying
quiz.explanation: From their side, your 6 is a 9. Both views can make sense.

quiz.question: Why did Adeel accept part of the blame for the slap?
options: He had embarrassed the student in front of everyone
quiz.explanation: He had announced the student's failed result in a crowded canteen. Seeing that helped him learn.

lessons.title: The chemistry of thank you
keyIdea: Gratitude is not only good manners. When you thank someone, the brain releases dopamine, the same reward chemical you feel when you win something.
Gratitude is also linked to serotonin, which lifts your mood, and to lower levels of cortisol, the stress hormone.
Both people gain: the one you thank feels good, and so do you. Noticing what you already have builds the habit.
lessons.action: Thank three people today by name and say exactly what they did, for example: "Thank you for lending me your racket yesterday." One of them should be someone at home.
lessons.reflectionQuestion: Whom did you thank today, and how did they react?

quiz.question: Which reward chemical does the brain release when you say thank you?
quiz.explanation: Adeel calls dopamine the first 'molecule of gratitude': the same reward chemical as winning a trophy.

quiz.question: Gratitude is linked to lower levels of which stress hormone?
quiz.explanation: Cortisol rises under stress. Serotonin, which rises with gratitude, helps keep it down.

quiz.question: Who feels good when you thank someone for a favour?
quiz.explanation: In the racket example, both people get a small dopamine boost.
